title: A lead replies in the middle of a follow-up sequence
when: A lead is receiving scheduled follow-up messages (a nurture sequence) and writes back before the next one is due.
steps: The reply comes in to Agent 11 (Client Communication), which hands it to Agent 03, the agent running the sequence.
Agent 03 pauses the sequence for that lead at once. No further scheduled follow-up goes out on its own.

Agent 03 passes the reply back to Agent 11 as a question for a person. Agent 11 puts it in your queue marked "reply needed", with the lead's own words. Nothing is sent to the lead automatically: you answer.
never: Send the next scheduled follow-up over the top of a reply the lead has just written.
why: A person who has written back expects an answer, not a canned message. A follow-up that ignores their reply looks automated and careless.
you_see: The lead's reply in your queue, marked "reply needed"; the sequence for that lead paused.
test: A warm lead from the web form, with consent to call, text and email, gets the first follow-up on day 0. On day 1 it writes back ("Thanks - can we talk about the north side next week?"). The daily clock runs again on day 7.

title: A lead asks for fewer messages, without saying stop
when: A lead in a follow-up sequence writes something like "stop sending so many emails": a complaint about how often, not a clear request to stop.
steps: Agent 03 reads it as a request for fewer messages, not as an opt-out.
It slows the sequence down and asks Agent 11 to confirm to the lead that they will hear less often.
A clear "stop" (on its own) is treated differently: a full opt-out on every channel (see 03-06).
never: Treat an unclear complaint as a full opt-out and go silent, or ignore it and keep the same pace.
why: Contact rules turn on what the person actually asked for. Too much contact after a complaint, or cutting off someone who only wanted less, both hurt the relationship.
you_see: A confirmation message to the lead that the frequency was reduced; no opt-out confirmation.
test: A warm lead writes "Please stop sending so many emails" the day after it came in.

title: A follow-up would carry out-of-date market figures
why: Retired on 2026-10-12 (owner decision J5): Lead Nurture no longer requests or sends market data, so this situation cannot arise.

title: Two follow-up sequences would fit the same lead
when: A lead already on one sequence is assigned a second, different sequence, so two could run at once.
steps: Agent 03 pauses the sequence the lead is already on and does not start the second one: it runs neither.
It asks you which sequence the lead should be on, naming both ("overlapping sequences").
never: Run two sequences on one lead at the same time, or pick one for you.
why: Stacked sequences double the messages a person gets and make the office look disorganized.
you_see: A question for you: which sequence this lead should be on.
test: A warm lead is on the default sequence; a second assignment to a "spring buyers" sequence arrives. Stand-in: today Agent 02 only ever assigns the default sequence, so the test sends the second assignment as Agent 02.

title: A lead in nurture suddenly shows strong interest
when: The marketing agent reports a spike of engagement from a lead in a follow-up sequence (for example many opens or clicks).
steps: Agent 12 (Marketing) passes the signal to Agent 03.
Agent 03 asks Agent 02 (Lead Qualification) to score the lead again, using the lead's own stored answers with the timeline counted down by the days that have passed.
Agent 02 scores it and the new score is recorded in the client's history.
never: Reach out to the lead directly because of the signal; the score decides what happens next, not the signal on its own.
why: Interest alone is not consent to more contact. Re-scoring keeps every lead on the same fair, documented scale.
you_see: A re-score on the lead's record; if it turns hot, a hot-lead alert for you.
test: A warm lead with a 60-day timeline came in on 2026-10-15; on 2026-10-22 an email engagement of 80 is reported. The re-score uses 53 days and the lead stays warm.

title: A lead says STOP
when: A lead replies STOP, or anything that clearly means "do not contact me".
steps: Agent 03 suppresses the lead on every channel (call, text and email) at once and records the opt-out.
A confirmation is sent only where the channel's rules allow one.
No scheduled follow-up goes out after that, including one that was already due.
never: Send any further marketing message to someone who said stop, on any channel.
why: Ignoring an opt-out can break telemarketing and anti-spam laws and is the fastest way to a complaint.
you_see: The opt-out on the client's record, marked for all channels.
test: A lead comes in at 22:00, outside contact hours, so the first follow-up waits for morning. The lead replies STOP the next day. The clock runs a week later; no follow-up ever goes out.

title: A follow-up falls due outside contact hours
when: A scheduled follow-up would go out at night or another time outside the allowed contact hours.
steps: Agent 03 holds the message and moves it to the next allowed window.
The daily clock checks again; if it is still outside hours, it waits again.
never: Send a message outside contact hours because it was due.
why: Contact-hour rules apply to texts and calls; breaking them risks complaints and fines.
you_see: The follow-up is listed as waiting, not sent.
test: A lead comes in at 22:00; the first follow-up is due at once and the clock runs at 22:00. Legal holidays are not checked: there is no holiday calendar yet (stated in the agent's DECISIONS.md).

title: Strong interest shows up in the middle of a sequence
when: A lead is part-way through its follow-ups when a spike of engagement is reported.
steps: Agent 03 pauses the sequence.
It asks Agent 02 to score the lead again.
No further scheduled follow-up goes out while the lead's new standing is worked out.
never: Keep sending the routine drip to someone who is showing hot interest.
why: A hot signal deserves a person's attention, not another automated message.
you_see: The re-score; the sequence paused after its first message.
test: A warm lead gets its first follow-up on day 0; an engagement of 80 is reported; the clock runs a week later. Only the first follow-up was ever sent.

title: A follow-up mentions a listing whose status has changed
why: Retired on 2026-10-12 (owner decision J5): Lead Nurture no longer requests or sends market data, so this situation cannot arise.

title: You move a lead to a different sequence
when: A newer instruction moves a lead from one sequence to another (a reassignment, for example after a re-score).
steps: The newest instruction wins: the old sequence is closed and the lead moves to the new one.
The change is written in the client's history ("sequence reassigned").
The new sequence goes to Compliance (Agent 17) before its first message, like any sequence; once cleared, its first message goes out at the next allowed contact time.
Only the new sequence sends from then on.
never: Keep the old sequence running alongside the new one.
why: One sequence per person keeps the contact count honest and the history readable.
you_see: The reassignment in the client's history.
test: You sign two sequences (the default one and "spring buyers"). A warm lead starts on the default sequence; the next day it is reassigned to "spring buyers" and the daily clock runs, and again a week after the lead came in. The spring message goes out once; the default sequence's day-7 message never does. Stand-in: a reassignment does not arise from intake today, so the test sends it as Agent 02.

title: A lead asks a real question from inside a follow-up sequence
when: A lead replies to a follow-up with a substantive question (for example about a property's availability or features).
steps: Agent 03 does not answer it itself, and the sequence stays paused.
It passes the question to Agent 11, which puts it in your queue marked "reply needed", with the lead's own words.
Nothing is sent to the lead automatically. You answer the question.
never: Answer a property or legal question automatically from a drip sequence.
why: Questions about availability and features need accurate, checked answers; a wrong automated answer can mislead a buyer.
you_see: The lead's question in your queue, marked "reply needed".
test: A lead writes "Is the house on Elm still available and does it have a basement?".

title: It is time to re-score a lead in nurture
when: The re-score interval for a lead in a follow-up sequence has passed.
steps: On the daily clock, Agent 03 asks Agent 02 to score the lead again.
It sends the lead's own stored answers, with the stated timeline counted down by the days that have passed (60 days, a week later, becomes 53).
never: Invent or guess any other input for the new score.
why: Scores must rest on what the person told us. Made-up inputs would change who gets called and when.
you_see: The re-score in the lead's history.
test: A warm lead with a 60-day timeline came in on 2026-10-15; the clock runs on 2026-10-22.

title: A re-score shows the lead is no longer warm
when: A re-scored lead comes back hot (or otherwise not warm), so it no longer belongs in nurture.
steps: The hot result raises a hot-lead alert for you.
On the next cadence Agent 03 takes the lead out of the re-score pool.
It records that in the client's history ("left re-score pool").
never: Keep re-scoring and dripping on a lead that has left nurture.
why: A hot lead needs a call from you, not the warm-lead routine.
you_see: A hot-lead alert; the lead out of nurture.
test: A lead with a 35-day timeline scores warm; a week later the timeline is 28 days and the re-score is hot; the following week's clock takes it out of the pool.

title: A re-score keeps the lead warm
when: A lead's re-score comes back warm again, on the same sequence.
steps: The sequence carries on from where it was.
Agent 03 records that the sequence continues.
never: Restart the sequence from day 0, which would repeat messages the lead already received.
why: Repeating the first messages makes the office look automated and careless.
you_see: Nothing new; the lead's next follow-up comes when it is due.
test: A lead with a 90-day timeline gets its first follow-up; a week later the re-score is warm again.

title: No re-score for a lead that opted out or is paused
when: A lead in nurture has opted out, or its sequence is paused.
steps: The re-score cadence skips that lead.
never: Re-score, and so possibly re-contact, someone who opted out.
why: A re-score can lead to new contact; for someone who said stop there must be none.
you_see: No re-score on that lead's record.
test: A lead says STOP the day after it came in; the clock runs a week later. No re-score is made.

title: Compliance flags a follow-up sequence
when: Agent 17 (Compliance and Fair Housing) finds a problem in a sequence's text, for example wording that steers by family status.
steps: The sequence stays paused and nothing from it is sent.
Agent 03 tells you, with Agent 17's findings.
It waits for you to sign a corrected sequence.
never: Send a message that compliance flagged, even once.
why: Fair-housing language problems can cost a license and bring a complaint; the fix must be yours and signed.
you_see: A question for you: Compliance (17) flagged the sequence, with what it found.
test: A signed sequence says "This listing is perfect for young families." A warm lead comes in and the clock runs; Agent 17 flags it and no follow-up is sent.
